title: ‘The Riverbank,’ ‘Elza’ Top Rio Film Festival Awards as ‘On Behalf of My Son,’ ‘The French Teacher’ and ‘London’ Scoop Key Prizes
description: Enock Carvalho and Matheus Farias’ Locarno-winning “The Riverbank” has taken Best Fiction Feature Film at this year’s Rio Film Festival, with Eryk R
body:
Enock Carvalho and Matheus Farias’ Locarno-winning “The Riverbank” has taken Best Fiction Feature Film at this year’s Rio Film Festival, with Eryk Rocha’s “Elza” scoring Best Documentary Feature Film. The awards were handed out tonight at an imposing ceremony at Rio de Janeiro’s legendary Odeon cinema.

	“The Riverbank” is set in Recife and follows young cleaner Izaquiel (Caique Copque), whose nightly search for intimacy leads him to magnetic fisherman Jeremias (Ítalo Martins). As violence closes in, both embark on a journey into the depths of the mangroves, where reality and myth intertwine, exposing the invisible structures of power that govern their world. This is the duo’s directorial feature debut, and it comes a few months after Farias won a Platino Award for his editing of Kleber Mendonça Filho’s Oscar-nominated “The Secret Agent.”
	

	“Elza” marks the follow-up to Rocha’s “The Falling Sky,” which premiered to great acclaim at Directors’ Fortnight. The film is a comprehensive documentary about one of Brazil’s most renowned singers and public figures, Elza Soares. Drawing on rare archival materials and intimate conversations between Soares and the director during the final years of her life, “Elza” traces the icon’s seven-decade career while revealing the many facets of the woman behind the legend. The project comes with the backing of high-calibre partners, including Aruac Filmes (“Cinema Novo”), Maria Farinha Filmes (“The Beginning of Life”), Globo Filmes (“I’m Still Here”), RAI Cinema and Gullane+.
	

	Other major Brazilian films of the year have also taken top awards, including Gabriel Martins’s Toronto-selected “On Behalf of My Son,” Venice-selected “London” by Victor di Marco and Márcio Picoli, and Ricardo Alves Jr.’s “The French Teacher,” which just bowed at San Sebastián.

	This year’s Premiére Brasil jury was presided over by veteran “La Bola Negra” producer Esther García and also included co-director of programming at the Berlinale, Jacqueline Lyanga; French producer Sophie Erbs; composer Flavia Tygel; and casting director Marcela Altberg.

	The New Trends jury was presided over by director and editor Karen Harley; screenwriter Maira Oliveira; producer Dora Amorim; director and screenwriter Guto Parente. The Felix Jury, dedicated to films broaching LGBTQIA+ issues, was presided over by lawyer Ericka Gavinho; director and screenwriter Clara Anastacia; cultural critic Guilherme Terri, also known as Rita Von Hunty; filmmaker Vita; and cultural programmer Rodrigo Gerace.

	See full list of winners below:

	Premiére Brasil

	Supporting Actress: Renna Costa, Artia and Ísis Broken, for “The Riverbank”Screenplay: “On Behalf of My Son,” Gabriel Martins

	Editing – ex aequo: Cristina Amaral, Fabio Meira and Juliano Castro, “A Extraordinária Vida de Vera Valdez” and Cristiane Oliveira and Tula Anagnostopoulos, “Foi Ali Guardar o Coração na Geladeira”

	Cinematography: Luciana Baseggio, “The Riverbank”

	Art Direction: Ana Paula Cardoso, “Funk”

	Costume Design: Samy Sill, “London”

	Sound Design: Moabe Filho, Guma Farias, Daniel Turini and João Victor Coura, “The Riverbank”

	Original Score: Florencia Di Concilio, “The French Teacher”
	

	Jury Award: “O Filho da Puta,” dir. Erica Maradona, Tania Anaya, Otto Guerra and Sávio Leite

	Documentary Feature – Audience Award: “Fui Olhar Você Dormir,” dir. Anna Azevedo

	Fiction Feature – Audience Award: “On Behalf of My Son,” dir. Gabriel Martins

	Novos Rumos (New Trends)

title: How Busan Title ‘Selvi’ Turns a Nurse’s Working Hours Into an Endurance Test
description: A homecare nurse whose working day stretches from 12 hours to 72 sits at the center of “Selvi,” the first feature from Tamil filmmaker Sailesh Rathn
body:
A homecare nurse whose working day stretches from 12 hours to 72 sits at the center of “Selvi,” the first feature from Tamil filmmaker Sailesh Rathnakumar, which premieres in the Busan International Film Festival’s Vision–Asia section.

	Anjali Patil plays the title role and produces through her banner Anahat Films. Rathnakumar wrote the screenplay with cinematographer Bargav Sridhar, and Sreekar Prasad edited the film.


	Selvi hopes to qualify as a nurse and eventually work in Singapore. When Kavitha, a friend since childhood, attempts suicide, Selvi takes over her shifts on top of her own and spends her days moving between private homes, caring for families who know little about her.
	

	“For someone like Selvi, a crisis doesn’t necessarily arrive as one dramatic event,” Rathnakumar tells Variety. “It develops through a series of working hours, additional responsibilities and small compromises that gradually become unbearable.”

	The jump from 12 to 24, 48 and then 72 hours gave the story its shape, he says. As the clock runs, Selvi is always on hand for someone else and has less and less time to be a person in her own right.

	The film opens on a beach, with Selvi and her friends flying kites, before moving into domestic interiors where her world narrows. “With the kites, I wanted to show the possibility of looking upwards, of imagining something beyond the immediate circumstances of one’s life,” Rathnakumar says.

	The production took its time finding homes that felt lived in and signaled the class of the families inside them. “Selvi can be essential to a family’s everyday life without ever being treated as someone who belongs to it,” he says.
	

	Most of the nurses the director has met came from rural villages to the cities for work. He sees a pecking order within the care sector, where some workers have the training and means to go abroad while others stay stuck in insecure jobs doing intimate, demanding work with little recognition.

	Because Sridhar co-wrote the script, the camera plan was baked in from the writing stage. The film never leaves Selvi’s point of view, and the audience learns things only when she does.

	Prasad came aboard at the script stage. At their first meeting, the editor flagged scenes that could go without harming the story, which saved the production time and money, Rathnakumar says. The director shot some of them anyway. None made the final cut.

	A Prague Film School alumnus, Rathnakumar began his career doing sound and music supervision for veteran Indian editor B. Lenin.

	For Patil, Selvi’s habit of putting her own plans on hold struck close to home. After finishing her postgraduate studies in design and direction at the National School of Drama in 2010, she drifted into acting and became one of her family’s main earners. She launched Anahat Films in 2021 intending to write and direct, then spent its first five years producing for other filmmakers.

	“Somehow our ambitions grow around circumstances like fungi,” Patil says. “Also, culturally, in Indian society, this behavior is celebrated. Keeping others before oneself to the point of absolute exhaustion. We are surrounded by so many Selvis, men and women alike.”

	The shoot couldn’t run in sequence and was organized by location instead, so Patil tracked her own makeup, hair, body and voice continuity across Selvi’s decline, leaning on continuity photos and long rehearsals with the ensemble. “I love being that human thermostat for the film,” she says.

	Wearing both hats came at a cost. The final scene was shot on Marina Beach at the end of a rough day, in a window of just a few hours. Patil was preoccupied with whether the production could afford to return if they missed it, and by the last take the light had gone. Rathnakumar and Sridhar told her they had what they needed, but she wasn’t satisfied.

	“I remember walking away hurriedly on Marina Beach, sobbing in frustration, hiding from the crew, thinking that, as a producer, I couldn’t even afford to give myself a proper time for the film’s end close-up shot,” Patil says.
	

	The actor, whose credits include “Naa Bangaaru Talli,” “Newton” and “Kaala,” co-produced “The Moogai,” which played Sundance in 2024, and “The Shadowbox,” which played Berlin in 2025. “Selvi” was presented as a work-in-progress at the Hong Kong-Asia Film Financing Forum in March and drew backing from the Red Sea Fund.

	International funding, Patil says, means long waits, complicated contracts and co-production treaties, and Indian filmmakers end up chasing the same grants as professionals from wealthier countries. “There is already an undisclosed disparity right there that nobody can talk about,” she says. “And honestly, a lot of times, I feel people still don’t know how to distribute independent Indian films in many parts of the world.”

	Rathnakumar points to character-led Tamil films such as “Maharaja,” “Meiyazhagan,” “Vaazhai” and “Lubber Pandhu,” which found audiences alongside star vehicles like “Amaran.” “I think the challenge for independent cinema is not necessarily whether audiences are willing to watch these films, but whether the films can reach them,” he says.

	Patil, who has worked in Hindi, Marathi, Telugu and Tamil-language cinema, says Tamil filmmaking has made room for independent voices over the past two to three years, calling it “very, very hopeful for all of us.”

	Next up, Rathnakumar is producing Patil’s feature “Average Girl,” the short “Florescence” and Sridhar’s directing effort “Goliath.” He is also developing “Uneventful Death of Mr. Srinivasan,” a comedy about a family whose celebrations turn to mourning when a 70-year-old man dies a day after his Bheema Radha Shanthi ceremony.

	Patil, meanwhile, plans to disappear after Busan to work full-time on a speculative sci-fi script she has been developing for six years. “I won’t be postponing my ambitions like Selvi,” she says.

title: ‘Bedford Park’ Star and Busan Juror Moon Choi on Locking Away Her Trophies and Plotting a Screen Version of a Molière-Winning Play
description:
For several years after the biggest run of her career, Moon Choi, known in Korea as Choi Hee-seo, kept her trophies out of sight.

	The haul was sub
body:
For several years after the biggest run of her career, Moon Choi, known in Korea as Choi Hee-seo, kept her trophies out of sight.

	The haul was substantial. Her turn as Japanese anarchist Kaneko Fumiko in “Anarchist from Colony” swept Korea’s new actress prizes, and her lead role in independent feature “Our Body,” which bowed in Toronto, earned her Busan International Film Festival’s Actress of the Year honor in 2018. By her own count, two films brought her 14 awards in a single year. She was around 30.
	

	“Some years passed, and I put the trophies in the cabinet. I didn’t want to have them displayed because whenever I saw them displayed somewhere, I kind of felt pressure,” Choi tells Variety. “I felt like I had to prove something to show them that I was worth it.”


	“I felt that being successful at a young age can do some bad things to you. It didn’t make me feel proud, but it actually kind of made me feel crestfallen because I felt like I had to reach a height that goes beyond those awards,” she says.

	What followed was a stretch she describes candidly: more independent films, Korean TV series that “flopped really badly” and film “A Girl with Closed Eyes” with Kim Minha that still has no release date two years after its Busan premiere. Through all of it, she was waiting for “Bedford Park.”

	Choi is now back in Busan in a different role, sitting on the seven-member jury for the festival’s competition section, which is only in its second year. Zhang Yimou presides over a panel that also includes Bi Gan, Kei Ishikawa, July Jung, Vietnamese producer Tran Thi Bich Ngoc and Kazakh actor Samal Yeslyamova. “Bedford Park” is also in town, screening in the Flash Forward section.
	

	“I don’t have the pressure that I need to prove anything to anybody,” Choi says of returning as a juror. “I’m kind of feeling like a student trying to learn from all these films that I’m going to be watching alongside amazing people like Zhang Yimou and Bi Gan.”

	Her yardstick for the competition comes from Asghar Farhadi’s idea that a good film begins once the audience leaves the cinema. Two days before heading to Busan, she watched Lee Chang-dong’s “Possible Love,” starring her friend and stage partner Jeon Do-yeon, on the big screen with her father. Outside the theater, the pair argued over whether the film’s final shot of a full moon offers hope. Her father read the title as a paradox pointing to an impossible love; she saw the opposite.

	“I just felt so fulfilled because of those conversations I had with my father, which is rare,” Choi says. “I want to look for the films that leave us with these amazing questions as we exit the theater, rather than the films that I feel like that give us definitive answers.”

	As an actor, she adds, she will be watching for performances that linger “not because they were so perfect, but because they were so truthful in the moment.”

	Written and directed by Stephanie Ahn, “Bedford Park” follows Audrey (Choi), a Korean American physical therapist in New Jersey caught between her immigrant parents’ expectations and her own life. After her mother is hurt in a car accident, Audrey forms an unlikely bond with Eli (Son Suk-ku), the former wrestler who was behind the wheel. The film world premiered in Sundance’s U.S. Dramatic competition in January and won the Special Jury Award for Debut Feature. Sony Pictures Classics picked up worldwide rights during the festival, and the film has since played Toronto’s Discovery program.

	Choi auditioned seven years ago. Ahn sent her the full screenplay in advance, which she says is rare, and she finished it on her phone in one sitting. Audrey’s tug-of-war between being a dutiful Korean daughter and living for herself mirrored her own upbringing: Japan from the ages of nine to 12, two years in Seoul, then three in New Jersey. Back in Korea, classmates teased her as “the Japanese kid.”

	“It seemed like wherever I went, I didn’t belong anywhere because when I came back to Seoul from Japan or the U.S., people would view me as that girl from Japan, that girl from the U.S.,” Choi says. “Although I’m not a Korean American immigrant, I thought that I could resonate with that.”
	

	Audrey’s profession gave Choi another way into the character. “I felt like she had such a warm heart for others, but she didn’t know how to do that for herself,” she says, linking that to the value Korean and Japanese families place on self-sacrifice. “I think Audrey was fighting against that.”

	The film took years to finance. Choi was unknown in the U.S., Ahn was a first-time director coming from editing, and Eli was originally written as a white character, with names like Tom Hardy and Jake Gyllenhaal floated as a dream. COVID shut everything down. Four years in, the team shot a 15-minute short as a proof of concept for financiers.

	Choi showed it to Son, a friend of a decade from the days when they would drop off casting resumes together. By then he had broken out as a star, and he told her he would want the role if Eli were Korean American. She pitched the idea of rewriting Eli as a Korean American adoptee to Ahn, who met Son over Zoom and reworked the script for him. Son in turn brought in Hyundai Motor Company, which backed the film as its first investment in an independent feature, and Foster and Ahn made Choi an executive producer. Foster produces alongside Russ Krasnoff, Chris S. Lee, Theresa Kang, Son and Nina Yang Bongiovi, whose earlier Sundance launches include “Sorry to Bother You” and Rebecca Hall’s “Passing.”

	“They were kind enough and generous enough for me to be able to focus on acting on set,” Choi says. Post-production brought three-hour Zoom calls over cuts and music cues. “That was, I think, when I felt like, ‘Oh, this is what producing feels like.’”

	Watching the finished film at Sundance, she says, felt like “giving birth to something so valuable,” a sentiment Son shared.

	Choi has rarely followed the conventional path for a Korean actor. A voracious reader as a child, she kept looking for scripts that could surprise her. That didn’t always sit well with K-dramas and Korean commercial films, where with some scripts, she says, you know exactly what will happen on the next page. That choosiness earned her a reputation for “independent and artsy movies.” After New Jersey, she enrolled at Seoul’s Yonsei University to read journalism and English literature, spending her evenings training as an actor with its student theater club, and later took a year of acting courses at UC Berkeley on an exchange program. She is also the author of a collection of short stories and poems. Along the way she appeared in Bong Joon Ho’s “Okja” and shot a two-hour feature in Gangneung with Japanese actor Joe Odagiri, who she says came to Korea and worked for next to nothing.
	

	Choi recalls a conversation with Jeon in New York, where the pair recently closed the final leg of Simon Stone’s staging of “The Cherry Orchard.” The production premiered in Seoul in 2024 with Jeon and “Squid Game” actor Park Hae-soo, then toured Hong Kong, Singapore and Adelaide before landing at New York’s Park Avenue Armory in September.

	“She just held my hands, and she said, ‘Moon … I’m so happy for you, and just know that you are greater than what you think you are,’” Choi says.

	Choi already has one directing credit, “Bandi,” her short for the 2021 “Unframed” anthology, in which she, Son, Park Jeong-min and Lee Je-hoon each directed a short. Choi and Son also wrote theirs. She says she never set out to direct and writes screenplays mainly for the pleasure of it.

	A new project may change that. Choi has signed on to lead a Korean stage adaptation of “Une histoire d’amour,” the play by French writer-director and actor Alexis Michalik that follows a lesbian couple’s attempt to have a child. The play premiered in 2020, picked up a Molière for its staging that year, and Michalik has since made it into a film. Choi will perform it in Seoul next year, and after a Zoom call with Michalik she has his blessing to option it for a screen version she pictures in Brooklyn.

	“Should I direct it, produce it? I’m not sure,” Choi says. What she does know is that she wants to write the screenplay herself, which she says “would kind of give me an idea if I want to produce it, or act in it, or direct it.”

	The global reach of K-pop and series like “Squid Game” has opened doors for Korean actors abroad, Choi says, but whether they can act in English remains the limit. Choi now acts in English, Korean and Japanese, but she only started learning English at 15, and Ahn hired a dialect coach for both leads so they would sound like Korean Americans from New Jersey. “I know I can do it because I’ve done it once,” she says.

	At home, she sees Korean cinema in recovery but leaning hard on genre, particularly horror, a pattern she also noticed in Los Angeles meetings. Park Chan-wook and Lee Chang-dong have delivered new films in back-to-back years, and she points to Na Hong-Jin and Byun Sung-hyun among those who followed them. But she wants more filmmakers her own age, in their late 30s or early 40s, and singles out Son, who runs his own production company and is writing his first feature.
	

	She feels a responsibility there too, she says, “because I produce now as well, I can probably be the forefront of that, because it’s generation, right? Who do we have after Lee Chang-dong and Park Chan-wook?”

	For now, Choi is on the festival circuit with “Bedford Park” and hunting for an English-language role. She signed with Gersh and management company Cognition six months ago and has been auditioning and sending self-tapes since.

	“I am a total newcomer in Hollywood,” she says.

	And the screen version of “Une histoire d’amour”? “I don’t know, it’s going to take 10 years, maybe.”

title: Polygamy, Ghosts and Grief Collide in ‘Marlina’ Director Mouly Surya’s Busan Asian Project Market Drama ‘The Wife Who Can See Dead People (Or Jinn)’
description: A young bride who sees ghosts joins a polygamous Muslim household and forms a bond with one of her husband’s other wives in “The Wife Who Can See De
body:
A young bride who sees ghosts joins a polygamous Muslim household and forms a bond with one of her husband’s other wives in “The Wife Who Can See Dead People (Or Jinn),” the new project from Indonesian director Mouly Surya (“Marlina the Murderer in Four Acts”). 

	The project is part of the Asian Project Market, which runs within the Busan International Film Festival’s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM).


	Gadis, 20, has just been brought home as the fourth wife of 50-year-old Abi. When she confides that ghosts appear to her, he tells her the dead cannot become ghosts in Islam, only jinn, spirits able to take many shapes, including those of people who have died. Of the three earlier wives and their kids, Gadis is drawn to Indah, the third wife, 35, and her seven-year-old son Firman. Indah teaches her how to run the house and even what to do in the marital bed, and Gadis looks after Firman, the one person who takes her ghost stories seriously. With Abi away overseas, Firman disappears, and Gadis and a motley band of ghosts help Indah look for him. When the boy’s body turns up by a river, the wives’ sisterhood is split between doing what feels right and following their husband’s wishes and Islamic tradition.
	

	Surya says the subject is personal. Members of her immediate family have multiple wives, and a close friend claims to see ghosts. “These are stories that are very close to me personally but one I always have questions for,” she says.

	The film sits on a set of contradictions, Surya says. Indonesia has the largest Muslim population in the world without being an Islamic state, and while its people believe in ghosts, the Quran has no such concept. Scripture permits men to take several wives, but Indonesian law does not recognize those unions. Watching polygamous families, Surya says, stirs pity, judgment and empathy in her, as well as fascination with the camaraderie, rivalry and sisterhood between the women. “There is a unique, somewhat bittersweet love between them, in a young woman yet to find her own footing such as Gadis or one with broken dreams like Indah,” she says.
	

	The project is mid-development, with a first draft of the screenplay complete, and is now in financing as the team applies for funds and co-production partners.

	Producers Gita Fara and Rama Adi say that since “Marlina,” they have pushed the craft of their storytelling and production further. This time they are after something more intimate and grown-up, closer to their earlier work, while keeping Surya’s visceral style: a grounded, moving drama laced with strange moments that can be thrilling, funny and haunting.

	They also point to the husband at the story’s center, a man who works hard to provide for and protect his family while attempting the impossible task of treating every wife fairly and equally. “Without trying to justify, we want to show polygamy beyond prejudices and visualize how they live with each other, facing tragedy, challenges, and things that are a little out of ordinary,” they say.

	In Busan, the producers want to meet potential co-production and sales partners and take the film’s first step onto the international stage. Fara is also at this year’s APM as a producer on Reza Rahadian’s “Casparina.”

title: Reza Rahadian Turns His Grandmother’s Decades in Exile Into Busan Asian Project Market Drama ‘Casparina’
description: A journalist stripped of her Indonesian citizenship in 1965 comes home decades later to children who grew up without her in “Casparina,” the second
body:
A journalist stripped of her Indonesian citizenship in 1965 comes home decades later to children who grew up without her in “Casparina,” the second feature from actor-director Reza Rahadian, inspired by the life of his grandmother Francisca Casparina Fanggidaej. 

	The project is part of the Asian Project Market, which runs within the Busan International Film Festival’s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM).


	In the film, Rina is driven into exile for opposing the government. Thirty-four years on, a letter tells her the old regime has collapsed and she is free to come home. Torn, she goes back to her children Andi and Lila, now grown and settled into lives that never included her. As she works through their hurt and resentment over the years she was gone, mother and children slowly find their way back to each other, and they come to understand what she gave up for her country and her family.
	

	Rahadian says he was drawn to a story of motherhood told through children whose mother was missing from their lives, set in a moment when a person’s citizenship could be taken away suddenly, by force and without warning. The separation, he says, kept his grandmother and her children apart for 32 years. “This is for me a very important story,” he says.

	He hopes viewers come away understanding that hard choices carry a price, and that they are sometimes driven by forces a person cannot see. He also wants audiences to grasp, in his words, “what it means to be a mother that is absent for 32 years,” and what it meant for her children to be unable to say openly who their mother was, because doing so could have put their lives at risk.
	

	Producers Arya Ibrahim and Gita Fara describe the project as a story of the political upheaval of 1965, which tore families apart and left people who lost their citizenship living as exiles. According to the producers, Casparina was in Beijing representing Indonesia at an international forum when her citizenship was revoked over her opposition to the new regime. She left six children behind and spent 32 years in exile, first in Beijing and later in the Netherlands, before the family reconnected.

	For the producers, stories like hers explain much about Indonesian history and identity. They call Casparina “a victim of an era” and see the film as a reminder not to repeat the same mistakes.

	Rahadian’s first feature as director, “On Your Lap,” won four prizes at the Busan festival’s Vision awards in 2025, including the audience award and the Fipresci award.

	“Casparina” is in the early stages of scriptwriting. In Busan, the producers hope to meet potential partners and collaborators, film funds and co-production opportunities.

title: Sylvia Chang Backs Malaysian Grief Drama ‘One Fine Day,’ About a Family Undone by Their Daughter’s Murder, at Busan Asian Project Market
description: A family torn apart by the unsolved murder of their young daughter tries to keep living day to day in “One Fine Day,” a Malaysian drama from directo
body:
A family torn apart by the unsolved murder of their young daughter tries to keep living day to day in “One Fine Day,” a Malaysian drama from director Tan Seng Kiat with Asian film icon Sylvia Chang aboard as executive producer. 

	The project is part of the Asian Project Market, which runs within the Busan International Film Festival’s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM).

	After their nine-year-old girl is sexually assaulted and killed, a family of four becomes three. With the case still open, the father fixates on tracking down the killer, the mother seeks solace in religion and their teenage son is weighed down by an untruth he has kept to himself. As life carries on around them, each grieves in their own way, and their sorrow pulls them apart even as they cling to what is left of the family. The filmmakers bill it as a film less about cracking a murder than about the ordinary days that come after a devastating loss.
	

	Tan drew on a real child murder in Malaysia. What lingered for him was not only the crime but the family it left behind. Public attention tends to fix on the culprit, the investigation and whether justice is done, he says, while the family still has to get up, eat and go to work in a world that carries on as if nothing has changed. “I wanted to explore how people live through something unbearable, while still having to face the ordinary routines of everyday life,” Tan says.


	He does not want the film to offer neat answers about grief. “Even within the same family, people can experience the same loss but cope with it in very different ways. They may love each other deeply, yet struggle to understand one another,” he says. Tan plans to trace those shifts through small moments, such as a family dinner, a conversation, a silence or the absence of something once there. “Above all, I hope audiences will see these characters not just as victims of tragedy, but as ordinary people trying to find a way to live with something they cannot change.”
	

	The script is in development after several years of work on the story, and the team is working with Malaysian and Taiwanese partners to push toward production while looking for more financing and international partners. Chang and producer Elyce Chin say Tan has wanted to make the film for over five years. They were moved by his sensitive handling of the material and his focus on the family’s everyday life, calling it a story “both deeply personal and universal.” Lim Shu Jia and E.N. Lee are also producers.

	In Busan, the team is looking for co-producers, financing and pre-sales, and hopes to test how a Malaysian story can connect with audiences from other cultures.

	Tan is also developing “The Supermum and Three Stickmen,” a comedy drawn from real events in which a single mom, saving up for her son’s wedding, is robbed of her nest egg and tries to win the stolen cash back. After so long immersed in grief, he says, he wants to look at relationships through humor and absurdity, though both films share his interest in how ordinary people react when life takes a sudden turn.

title: Locarno Title ‘Rapture’ Director Dominic Sangma Confronts Unregulated Stone Mining in Busan Asian Project Market Drama ‘Veil of Dust’
description: A villager maimed by a mining blast and his wife’s fight for compensation open up a story of exploitation, complicity and indigenous belief in “Veil
body:
A villager maimed by a mining blast and his wife’s fight for compensation open up a story of exploitation, complicity and indigenous belief in “Veil of Dust,” the new project from “Rapture” director Dominic Sangma. 

	The project is part of the Asian Project Market, which runs within the Busan International Film Festival’s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM).

	When an explosion rips through the hills, 35-year-old Nengsal is dug out of the debris having lost a leg. His wife Ajin, 32, sets out to win compensation but runs into a system that thrives on exploiting people and keeping them quiet. The headman is compromised, an NGO in the area is pursuing its own politics, and the man running the mine discloses that Nengsal was never on the books, leaving workers like him invisible on their own land. Through the couple’s children, 12-year-old Kasanchi and 10-year-old Miklu, the film moves into a mystical realm rooted in indigenous belief, as healer Rengin leads Miklu through an unsettling ritual on a bird meant to “transfer” his father’s wound. When an unplanned blast kills a boy from the village, the elders take advance compensation to keep the peace. With Nengsal pleading with Ajin to end his pain and her fight for justice going nowhere, she turns to the rare herbs in her garden, which can both heal and harm.
	

	Stone mining has surfaced in Sangma’s earlier films, but here it takes center stage, and the urgency of the subject led him to pause the final film of his village trilogy. The blasts, the shaking ground, wrecked homes and farms, and villagers killed in mine accidents are part of his childhood memories, and the mining is still going on. It had been normal for so long that he never felt the need to address it, he says, until a recent stay in the village, where he saw landslides, cracked houses and mining edging closer to the main settlement.
	

	“To an outsider, unregulated mining might seem like a mere environmental issue. But to those of us who live in its shadow, it doesn’t just erode the soil – it erodes the soul,” Sangma says.

	The father of a young daughter, Sangma says he hopes speaking out will make the village a slightly better home for her. The elders have stayed quiet, perhaps because they never saw mining as a problem or because it has fed many of them, and the deeper he went, the more tangled it became. “In a way villagers were the part of the reason why it continues for so long,” he says.

	Sangma calls the film “a microcosm to what we are doing to the mother earth with our greed” and hopes it will nudge audiences to care a little more for the planet.

	Producer Xu Jianshang, who produced Sangma’s debut “Ma’ama” and “Rapture,” says the director is moved by his community’s suffering and that his very local concerns speak to the wider world. “There is beauty and grace in his image making and as a producer I feel we need to support more such voices,” she says.

	“Rapture,” the second film in Sangma’s trilogy, premiered at Locarno in 2023 and won the cultural diversity award at the Asia Pacific Screen Awards. “Ma’ama” won best cinematography at the Shanghai International Film Festival and best film at the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival. 

	“Veil of Dust” is in development, and in Busan the team is raising money and seeking co-production partners and backers who share the director’s vision.

title: ‘The Sea Speaks His Name’ Review: Absorbing Indonesian Political Thriller Is an Ode to Disappeared Activists
description: In an age where some call themselves activists merely through social media posting, stories of the dangers, consequences and occasional, very hard-w
body:
In an age where some call themselves activists merely through social media posting, stories of the dangers, consequences and occasional, very hard-won rewards of boots-on-the-ground political activism have additional potency. Though Yosep Anggi Noen‘s compellingly angry and anguished “The Sea Speaks His Name” is set predominantly in the 1990s, chronicling grassroots student resistance to Indonesian military dictator Suharto in the fraught final years of his punishing New Order regime, this impassioned political thriller is as universally timely as it is historically specific and eye-opening. It bears a message for anyone moved to act or speak out against corrupt institutions and administrations in the present day.
	

	That message isn’t a blandly inspirational or emptily motivational one. Characters suffer and sacrifice much for their principles in “The Sea Speaks His Name,” and the film poignantly honors those who work towards instigating change without ever getting to see the outcome. But it’s not without hope either, gradually bringing its community-minded story to “a small light at the end of a dark tunnel.” 


	Playing in competition at the Busan Film Festival, Noen’s sixth feature returns him to the subject and milieu of his Locarno-premiered 2016 film “Solo, Solitude,” a biopic of the protest poet Widji Thukul, who has exiled for his anti-Suharto activism. Adapted from a celebrated and widely translated novel (with the same English title) by Leila S. Chudori, who also acts as a producer here, “The Sea Speaks His Name” paints on a broader canvas to rousing effect. It grabs viewers by the heart in comparable fashion to “I’m Still Here,” Walter Salles’ similarly urgent and sorrowful chronicle of a forced disappearance in a military dictatorship. It won’t match that film’s profile, but global arthouse distributors should take an interest, and further festival play is a given.
	

	The film happily reunites Noen with Reza Rahadian, the charismatic lead of his 2024 Netflix crime drama “24 Hours With Gaspar,” and a sharp, emotionally engaged asset here. He plays Laut, an earnestly dedicated activist introduced in a heart-in-mouth prologue set in 1998: Preparing dinner in the midst of a power outage, he’s surprised when a group of government operatives crash his Jakarta apartment, seizing, restraining and removing him before he can say a word in his defence, as neighbors in his building look on anxiously. The agents address him as Amir Zein, but we soon learn that’s an alias; in a hopeless letter written from prison to his sister Asmara — epistolary narration drives much of the film’s action — he begins to tell his story.

	We rewind to 1991, where, as a fresh-faced university student in Yogyakarta, Laut meets and falls in with magnetic campus firebrand Kinan (Dian Sastrowardoyo), who leads a rebellious discussion group focused in particular on literature banned by the state: “In this country, books are threats,” he says in voiceover. Though not a complete naif — his father (Arswendy Bening Swara) is a journalist all too familiar with the ways of the government — Laut finds he can no longer ignore violent systems of state oppression; in time, he and Kinan, along with their cohorts, determine that discussion is no longer enough, and commit to a more actively radical student resistance movement.

	They soon learn that this is no game, and the dictatorships’s heavy-handed response to their activism requires Laut, like many others, to change his name and go into hiding. In stages, he is lost to his supportive but fretful family — Christine Hakim, standout star of fellow Busan competition title “Ibuku,” plays his mother — and after his 1998 capture, the film’s focus shifts to their pained but persistent efforts to find him, or at least to piece together his story. As Asmara, the sibling who gravely inherits his cause, Yunita Siregar gives a lovely, stoically moving performance; if the film misses Laut’s force of personality when he disappears from the narrative, so do all those connected to him.

	“The Sea Speaks His Name” is assembled in straightforward but effectively sweeping fashion, with Dinda Amanda’s nimble editing making light work of a 134-minute running time, and ceding the drama to stirring archival footage at the close. Batara Goempar’s ambiently somber lensing, meanwhile, reinforces the film’s thriller trappings, often highlighting faces and bodies in pools of darkness, as befits a tense, tightly wound tale of people confining themselves to the shadows for their survival.

title: Andrew Garfield Reacts to Oscar Buzz as ‘Artificial’ Gets Resounding London Reception: ‘So Flattered That Anyone Is Going to See This Film in the First Place’
description: “Artificial” isn’t hitting theaters until December, but Andrew Garfield is already sparking Oscar buzz for his performance as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.
body:
“Artificial” isn’t hitting theaters until December, but Andrew Garfield is already sparking Oscar buzz for his performance as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

	Luca Guadagnino‘s tech tale, which follows the five-day period in 2023 when Altman was fired and then rehired, earned rave reviews after its world premiere at New York Film Festival last week. Both Garfield and “Anora” breakout Yura Borisov — who plays Ilya Sutskever, the OpenAI co-founder who ousted Altman — have now entered the awards race, with Garfield campaigning in supporting and Borisov in lead. 
	

	Speaking to Variety on the red carpet at its London Film Festival premiere on Sunday, Garfield — who has been Oscar-nominated twice but never won — reacted humbly to the praise. “As I’m getting older, I’m starting to understand that the things outside of ourselves, we just have no control over. And the only consistent thing for me is trying to make work that I feel proud of,” he said. “I feel really, really proud of this film … It was a really, really intense shoot. And then I’m so flattered that anyone is going to see this film in the first place, let alone talk so nicely about it. That’s my genuine response. I try and keep it in that perspective.”


	Borisov, who was up for a supporting actor Oscar for “Anora” in 2024, chimed in with: “It’s a miracle!” 

	He added, “It’s unpredictable, I don’t know what to say. I’m really curious how people will feel. I’ll see what happens.” 

	Besides Garfield and Borisov, “Artificial” also stars Monica Barbaro as former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, Ike Barinholtz as Elon Musk and Mark Rylance as “Godfather of AI” Geoffrey Hinton. All were on hand for the London premiere.
	

	Asked about the timeliness of the movie, Garfield said: “It’s here, it’s now. And the timing couldn’t be more exciting and important, I think, because it’s about the figures that are in the news right now. Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, Elon and all the major players that are kind of governing and holding the reins of this new technology, or occasionally losing the reins of this new technology. It’s really about that.” 

	Added Barbaro, “I think AI is being used everywhere, in every industry. It’s kind of the No. 1 conversation right now, and I think that’s important to sort of question the motives of those who have created that kind of technology that has that much power.”

	Even before its debut, “Artificial” has been the subject of much discussion as Amazon MGM Studios dropped the film in June, shortly after Amazon invested $50 billion in OpenAI. Neon then picked it up for distribution and is mounting its awards campaign.

	In an interview with Vanity Fair last week, Altman addressed the film for the first time and said that that he did not speak to anyone at Amazon about dropping the movie, including Jeff Bezos, and “I don’t know of anyone else who did.”

	He also revealed that the movie filmed outside of his house and claimed that he waved to Garfield, who he admitted did nail his walk and “quirky mannerisms.” Garfield confirmed to Variety that he doesn’t recall seeing Altman while filming.

	“I heard him say that and I was like, I would have remembered,” he said. “I was so aware of looking for him when we were shooting near his house and on those streets. I didn’t see him and I was very, very disappointed that I didn’t. It was thrilling, it was exciting and terrifying. We were right outside his house, but no, I didn’t see him.”

	Inside the Royal Festival Hall, Guadagnino introduced the film on stage alongside his cast as the crowd clapped rigorously in anticipation. Guadagnino, known for his stylistic and sexy films like “Call Me by Your Name” and “Challengers,” admitted that “Artificial” was “the most complicated movie to imagine because the world of the Silicon Valley is the least seductive visually.” 

	“I hope you will be seduced by the movie, though,” he continued. “It was a lot of research, very, very deep, extensive research. It was a great journey to understand the people and the places and infrastructure, and we tried to go for the most close attention to detail as possible.”
	

	Garfield said he found working with the director again to be “irresistible” after last year’s “After the Hunt.”

	“Luca is irresistible as a filmmaker, and Luca combined with such a juxtaposed world on its own is irresistible. Like, how is he going to make this erotic?” Garfield said. “You’ll see how he made it erotic. He finds the nooks and the crannies. It’s really a remarkable thing to work with Luca because he’s one of our radical film cinema artists.”

	Garfield also revealed that he also had an “old dangling thread” from “The Social Network,” in which he played Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin (and had a very memorable monologue), but was originally in the running to play Mark Zuckerberg. 

	“I had auditioned for Mark Zuckerberg and some other guy got it. But I was kind of told that I was going to play Mark Zuckerberg for a few weeks, it was dangled in front of me,” he said. “So I started immersing myself in Mark and then [producer] David Heyman called me to his office and said, ‘Well, there’s a better guy for it.’ … But I started to imagine myself into that responsibility, leading humanity into this next chapter and what it takes to take the burden of that responsibility. What kind of personality, what kind of facets does this person have, what kind of resilience a person has to have.”

	Garfield added of Altman: “I’m still deeply curious about Sam, he’s unfolding before our eyes as we speak and it’s kind of endlessly fascinating, like AI itself I guess.”

	Barinholtz brought some comedic relief by saying of playing Musk, “I had never heard of him. Just not a news guy!” 

	On a more serious note, he said that the film required him to separate the tech mogul’s present-day persona from how he was viewed when he co-founded OpenAI. 

	“I think we have the tendency to think about someone the most recently we saw them, and at that time, it was DOGE and chainsaws and kind of crazy behavior,” he said. “But this story takes place long before then, it takes place at this time where he really was looked at like a god, especially amongst these Silicon Valley people.”

	Barinholtz said Guadagnino helped get the actors into the spirit on set. “Every time Elon walked into the room, if one of the cast members was not in awe of him, Luca would come up like: ‘This is Elon Musk! You need to be like, oh my God!'” Barinholtz said, sparking laughter in the room.
	

	During the film, audience members both laughed and gasped in horror as the events of OpenAI’s founding and 2023 unraveling were brought to screen. As the credits rolled, enthusiastic clapping echoed throughout the Royal Festival Hall, making it clear that “Artificial’s” momentum would not be stopping in London.

	“Artificial” is set to debut in U.S. theaters on Dec. 25 and in the U.K. on Jan. 22.

schema.headline: Andrew Garfield Reacts to Oscar Buzz as ‘Artificial’ Gets Resounding London Reception: ‘So Flattered That Anyone Is Going to See This Film in the First Place’

title: Box Office Boom for China’s Women Directors Feeds New Parallax Films Pickups From Shao Yihui, Yin Lichuan and Yang Lina (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Three filmmakers at the forefront of China’s women-led cinema boom – Shao Yihui, Yang Lina and Yin Lichuan – have new titles on the slate of sales a
body:
Three filmmakers at the forefront of China’s women-led cinema boom – Shao Yihui, Yang Lina and Yin Lichuan – have new titles on the slate of sales agent Parallax Films, which is shopping them to buyers at the Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM) in Busan.

	In the short “Winning at Sleep,” Shao turns her satirical eye on meritocracy and the culture of constant competition. The story centers on an everyday girl who is handed an unlikely chance at glory through an unusual contest.
	

	“It’s OK” reteams Yang with Golden Horse winner Wen Qi (“Angels Wear White,” “The Bold, the Corrupt and the Beautiful”). Wen plays a young teacher dealing with an urgent health crisis, all while managing the unspoken connection she shares with her traditional mother. The dramedy takes on questions of womanhood and a woman’s control over her own body.


	Veteran director Yin’s “A Joke” is billed as the first Chinese feature to tackle sexual harassment in the workplace. It follows a sanitation worker who spends three years quietly collecting proof against her abusive boss, then joins forces with a young lawyer to expose him.

	The pickups ride a wave that began in 2021 with Shao’s breakout “B for Busy,” which opened the door for female-centered stories in China. Three years later, Yin’s “Like a Rolling Stone” and Shao’s second feature “Her Story” grossed more than RMB845 million ($118 million) combined at the domestic box office.

	“Her Story” went on to win best picture, best actress and best supporting actress at the 38th Golden Rooster Awards, mainland China’s government-backed film honors. Films by women directors have historically won few opportunities at the awards, making the haul a landmark for feminist filmmaking in the country.
	

	On the festival circuit, Luka Yuanyuan Yang’s documentary hybrid “Chinatown Cha-Cha” found similar success. Parallax credits a young female audience with growing clout for proving that films about gender roles, relationships and social pressure can pull in big numbers. Investors, studios and producers have since backed a broader range of women-led projects.

	A generation of female directors now works across both commercial and indie filmmaking, chasing box office and festival prestige at once. Alongside Shao and Yin, the group includes Yang (“Spring Tide,” “Song of Spring”), Teng Congcong (“Send Me to the Clouds,” series “To the Wonder”) and Vivian Qu (“Angels Wear White,” “Girls on Wire”).

	Parallax’s short film lineup also features “Our Secrets,” which took the Lights On Women’s Worth Award at Cannes’ La Cinef. “Scorching,” “Thirteenth Night” and “Fishtank” turn to fantasy to chart their characters’ interior lives. “Orlo With Karma” is a Tibetan coming-of-age romance from Kangdrun, director of “Linka Linka.”

	“Linka Linka,” which won the Firebird and Fipresci prizes at the Hong Kong International Film Festival, explores urban Tibetan youth culture today, while “100 Sunset” looks at the Tibetan diaspora in Canada. Anuparna Roy’s “Lovers in the Blue Night” won the Netpac Award at Venice. Documentary and hybrid titles about identity and family include “Masayume,” Visions du Réel winner “From Dawn to Dawn” and docufiction “Shanghai Daughter.” “Now I Met Her” and “Embers” sit at the commercial end of the slate.

title: Indigo Girls Mourn Death of Tour Bus Driver After Fatal Crash
description:
Indigo Girls
                          Mourning Beloved Tour Bus Driver After Fatal Crash
body:
Indigo Girls
                          Mourning Beloved Tour Bus Driver After Fatal Crash
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The Indigo Girls are mourning a heartbreaking loss on the road ... their longtime tour bus driver was killed in a crash in South Carolina, forcing the folk-rock duo to cancel upcoming shows.
      
    
            The driver -- identified by the band as Kirk -- was behind the wheel Friday morning when the bus slammed into a disabled tractor-trailer on Interstate 20 around 6 AM, according to authorities.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Kirk was the only person on the bus at the time ... neither Indigo Girls members Amy Ray and Emily Saliers nor any of their crew were onboard.
      

            The cause of the crash remains under investigation.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The "Closer to Fine" singers addressed the tragedy in an emotional statement ... saying Kirk had safely driven them thousands of miles over the years and had become a beloved part of their touring family.
      
    
            They wrote, "He was a joyful constant in our lives, and we will miss him dearly."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The duo canceled their Saturday show in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, and postponed Sunday's performance in Wilmington, North Carolina ... with decisions on additional tour dates still to come.
      
    
            Amy and Emily say they plan to return to the road when they're ready ... but for now, they're remembering the man who helped make their shows possible night after night.

title: Diane Keaton Remembered by Sarah Paulson One Year After Her Death
description:
Sarah Paulson on Diane Keaton
                          One Year Later and Still Missing You
body:
Sarah Paulson on Diane Keaton
                          One Year Later and Still Missing You
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 11, 2026
                            5:10 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Sarah Paulson is remembering her dear friend Diane Keaton on the one-year anniversary of her death ... sharing a sweet throwback photo of the two laughing together alongside Diane's daughter, Dexter White.
      
    
            The "American Horror Story" actress posted the pic to Instagram Sunday, showing the trio bundled up in winter clothes and having a blast ... with Diane throwing her hand in the air while Sarah cracks up beside her.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Sarah kept the caption short but heartfelt, writing ... "One year. Impossible. Laughing with you will always be what I remember most. I love you."
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported, Sarah was visibly emotional while discussing Diane's legacy just days after her death, calling her a dear friend and saying she was even more spectacular as a person than audiences knew her to be as an actress.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The two became close after working together on the 1999 movie "The Other Sister" ... building a friendship that lasted more than two decades.
      
    
            Diane died Oct. 11, 2025 at age 79 ... and her family later confirmed pneumonia was the cause of death.
      
    
            One year later, it's clear Sarah is holding tight to the happy memories ... especially all the laughs they shared.

title: Kelly Clarkson Responds to Brooklyn Store, Calls Owner a 'Liar' Over $15K Bird
description:
Kelly Clarkson
                          Strikes Back at Brooklyn Shop ...
                          C
body:
Kelly Clarkson
                          Strikes Back at Brooklyn Shop ...
                          Claims Battle Stems from $15K Bird
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 11, 2026
                            5:38 PM PDT
                                                                            
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Kelly Clarkson is firing back at a Brooklyn store owner, calling them a "liar" amid a dispute over an expensive singing bird sculpture she says she tried to buy.
      
    
      
      Cool, cool. Sure, it wasn’t for sale. That’s the narrative Art of Play is gonna go with 👍 so the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale whilst pointing to the price tag hanging on the wall with the title Singing Bird didn’t happen as you elevator eyed me saying in a condescending tone “yes, it’s for sale but it costs 15,000 dollars so if you’d like me to find something comparable for you I can.” That all never happened and now it’s not for sale. Okay, cool. So you’re not only rude, you’re also a liar. Got it ✅ 
And by the way, I obviously support small businesses because I was literally at a small business trying to purchase things. I love small businesses and know they are important and I always support them, but you don’t get a free pass to treat people less than in your store just because you are a small business. It’s not that hard to be kind. I never blast people but you my friend were an exception. 
Your store is really cool. 
Unfortunately, you aren’t.
              @kellyclarkson
          
  
    
            Kelly took to social media to slam Art of Play’s account of their interaction ... insisting the owner initially told her the piece was for sale for $15,000 before allegedly offering to find her something comparable.
      
    
            "That all never happened and now it’s not for sale. Okay, cool," Kelly wrote, accusing the owner of being rude and condescending ... before adding, "So you're not only rude, you're also a liar."
      

        Waiting for your permission to load the Instagram Media.
      
    
            The store has disputed her earlier version of events, saying the singing bird automaton, known as "Molly," is attached to the wall and used in magic shows ... and was never for sale.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Kelly also pushed back against any suggestion she doesn't support small businesses, saying she was literally shopping at one when the alleged incident happened, adding "You don’t get a free pass to treat people less than in your store just because you are a small business."
      
    
            The former "The Voice" judge ended her post with one final dig at the shop owner ... "Your store is really cool. Unfortunately, you aren’t."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            As we previously reported ... Kelly took to social media to describe an allegedly frustrating shopping experience at the Brooklyn store.
      
    
            Kelly claimed she traveled to the small shop intending to buy multiple items, only to feel an employee was steering her toward a cheaper alternative rather than taking her shopping plans seriously.
      
    
            The "Since You've Been Gone" singer described the moment as like "Julia Roberts character in Pretty Woman" and slammed the store for it's lack of hospitality.
      
    
            Now, the battle continues, and it looks like this shopping showdown is far from over.

title: Kelly Osbourne Says She's Gained Nearly 30 Pounds After Grief-Fueled Weight Loss
description:
Kelly Osbourne
                          Ozzy's Death Left Me Unable to Eat ...
body:
Kelly Osbourne
                          Ozzy's Death Left Me Unable to Eat ...
                          Now I'm Re-Gaining Weight
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Kelly Osbourne is opening up about her dramatic weight loss following the death of her father, Ozzy Osbourne ... revealing she's since gained nearly 30 pounds after grief left her barely able to eat.
      
    
            The reality star told The Sun she was shocked when she saw photos of herself at the BRIT Awards in February ... admitting she had no idea how thin she'd gotten.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            "I couldn't f***ing believe it," Kelly said ... adding she's gained 28 pounds in the six months since.
      

            Kelly insists she wasn't battling an eating disorder ... explaining her grief was so overwhelming that eating made her physically sick.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            At one point, she even visited Ozzy's grave with a candle, begging her late father to help her get better. The next day, her mom, Sharon Osbourne, introduced her to therapist Chris Miller ... whom Kelly credits with saving her life.
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported, Kelly has faced intense scrutiny over her appearance, repeatedly firing back at critics who've commented on her weight.
      
    
            And she's making some big life changes ... moving from Los Angeles to the English countryside with her 3-year-old son, Sidney, following her split from fiancé Sid Wilson.
      
    
            Kelly says she wants her son to have a stable childhood without worrying about school shootings ... and she's even joined his school's PTA.
      
    
            After a devastating stretch, Kelly says she's finally starting to feel like herself again.
